transcript:
Meeting header:
2026-09-10 14:00 PDT | Duration: 42m
Attendees: Sam Patel (Redwood AE), Riley Chen (Redwood SE), Alex Gomez (Redwood CSM) - Jared Lee (CTO, Monarch), Priya Nair (Head of ML), Marcus Rivera (Infra), Tina Hu (Product)

[00:00] Sam Patel: hey everyone, thanks for joining, we'll do a quick run through of the console tracing and request logs and focus on the debugging flow you asked about in the email. back of the room, riley will demo and i'll chime in on security and commercial bits

[00:22] Jared Lee: thanks sam. high level - our infra team wants to know if we can see the raw request path and the model decisions, and also what level of PII redaction we can get.

[00:35] Riley Chen: yeah absolutely, we'll show the trace view, how to pivot into request logs, and also show the request payload and how redaction works. quick note - some names may be slightly off in console screenshots, i've seen it say "Redwood Consolee" in older dev builds, so ignore that, haha

[01:05] Priya Nair: also want to know how easy it is to run a debug on a particular user session - like reproduce the request sequence and re-run with a diff model.

[01:22] Riley Chen: great, that's a common flow. i'll start by opening the tracing dashboard. (screen share) you'll see an overview of traces per route, latency distribution, and errors. clicking a specific trace expands a timeline with spans - the token generation spans, routing decisions, cache hits - the usual.

[01:55] [Riley shares screen]
[02:10] Riley Chen: here i click a failed trace. in the left panel you get metadata: route, model id, region, and request id. note - our UI sometimes abbreviates model names, you'll see e.g. "rw-bison-13b-q4" trimmed to "rw-bison-13b" in older logs, so cross-check with the trace id.

[02:40] Marcus Rivera: is that request id stable across retries?

[02:48] Riley Chen: yes we attach a root request id that persists across retries and fallbacks, and we surface child span ids for each attempt. that makes it easier to correlate retries with the eventual success or failure.

[03:12] Riley Chen: from the trace, you can click "Open request logs" which brings you to the request log entry for that request id. request logs include the raw request payload (if allowed by retention/redaction policies), headers, routing decisions, and server-side error messages.

[03:36] Jared Lee: about raw payload - can we restrict which fields are captured? we can't have full PAYLOADs stored for GDPR reasons.

[03:44] Sam Patel: yes, two levers - per-route redaction rules (regex/field lists) and automatic PII detection. we also have integration with your KMS so logs can be encrypted at rest and access audited. i'll share the security doc after this call.

[04:05] Priya Nair: for POC we'd like to see logs for 30 days and then have them archived to our S3. is that supported?

[04:13] Alex Gomez: yes; retention is configurable. for Private deployments you can push to your S3 or SIEM. Hosted has built-in retention tiers; we can set up a pipeline to push to your archive bucket during the POC.

[04:40] Riley Chen: jumping back to the UI - here's an error span with a model runtime error. you can expand the span to see error code, stack-ish trace, and server logs. caution: the transcript text in trace snippets can be noisy, e.g., "kv cache" sometimes transcribed as "k v cash" in the auto annotations.

[05:10] [Slight cross-talk, someone muting/unmuting]

[05:30] Tina Hu: can we search across traces for a specific user id?

[05:37] Riley Chen: yes, you can query by user_id, route, model, request_id, or arbitrary tags we attach. queries use a simple lucene-like syntax. i'll run a search now for user: "jlee_17" to show you.

[06:05] [Search executes]
[06:12] Riley Chen: results list shows matched traces and a quick stats pane. click one to jump straight to the trace. from there i can click floor "open raw request" - the raw payload shows up but with redaction markers for fields configured to be redacted.

[06:32] Marcus Rivera: about RBAC - which roles can view raw unredacted logs? we need separation of duties.

[06:40] Sam Patel: good Q. RBAC is per-team and per-env. you can restrict "logs:view_raw" to a specific role and require SSO + AIA approval. for Private customers we also support HSM/KMS-based envelope encryption so keys are customer controlled.

[07:05] Priya Nair: can you demo how to export a trace to our SIEM? we use Splunk.

[07:12] Riley Chen: sure - from trace detail there's an Export menu; you can push JSON to a webhook or to an S3 path we manage. i have an example export payload i'll paste to the chat. (pastes link) Deck: https://redwood.app/share/trace-export-example

[07:45] Jared Lee: will logs contain model tokenization details? we sometimes need raw token ids to debug hallucinations.

[07:53] Riley Chen: we capture token-level timing and token ids in verbose mode - this is off by default because of size. for POC we can enable verbose traces for selected routes so you get token-level info for a subset of traffic.

[08:20] Tina Hu: any latency impact when tracing is enabled?

[08:25] Riley Chen: tracing is asynchronous, minimal overhead. token-level verbose traces do add overhead and storage, but we run them sampled or on-demand. typical overhead is <5% for standard trace metadata.

[08:52] [Moderator note: Riley scrolling through trace timeline]

[09:10] Riley Chen: now i'll show an error-analysis workflow. we have a panel that aggregates error types by route and shows likely root causes. clicking into a cluster shows a basket of example traces, top stack traces, and correlated metrics (cpu, gpu, kv cache hit rates).

[09:36] Priya Nair: does it correlate with model rollouts - like i want to see errors introduced after a canary?

[09:42] Riley Chen: yes we tag traces with model version and rollout id. you can filter time windows and compare pre/post rollout. there's a builtin regression view we can wire into your alerting.

[10:05] Jared Lee: about alerts - do you support webhook alerts when error rate exceeds threshold?

[10:12] Alex Gomez: yep, threshold-based alerts, anomaly detection, and integrations with PagerDuty/Slack. alerts include links to example traces and a pre-populated runbook template if you want to triage.

[10:40] Marcus Rivera: so hypothetically if we see a PII leak in the logs, can we delete that single trace?

[10:48] Sam Patel: we support targeted deletion by request_id and also account-level retention and purge policies. for hosted accounts we can perform deletions and provide attestations; for Private we can give you direct control.

[11:15] Riley Chen: okay next i'll demo the request-logs query page. this is where you can run ad-hoc queries and export results. queries support time ranges, boolean logic, and aggregation. here's an example query - status: 5xx AND route: "/checkout" AND model: "rw-bison*"

[11:45] [Query runs]

[11:52] Riley Chen: results show 87 hits in the last 24 hours, top error messages, and a sample request payload for each. you can select a row and press "replay" to re-run the request against a staging model. note: replay respects redaction rules and your PII settings.

[12:20] Priya Nair: can we re-run with a patched prompt or different temperature?

[12:26] Riley Chen: yes, replay allows you to modify the payload (prompt, model, parameters) and replay in a sandbox environment. there's also a safety flag to mark replays as non-production.

[12:48] Jared Lee: what about production isolation? does replay hit prod models?

[12:53] Riley Chen: by default replay targets a staging endpoint; you can configure it to hit a canary model or a specific replica if you have dedicated capacity. we enforce permissions around who can trigger replay in prod.

[13:20] [Brief pause as Riley prepares an example replay]

[13:35] Riley Chen: here's a replay where i modify the prompt to add a guardrail and switch model to a smaller variant - run it now. (executes) result returns, you can compare outputs side-by-side and save the run as an artifact.

[14:00] Priya Nair: helpful. for POC we want to run a set of regression prompts against two model variants and capture traces for each - can the console orchestrate that?

[14:12] Riley Chen: the console has a small evaluation runner under the Optimize tab, but for larger evals we recommend our Optimize toolkit which can run batched evals and push traces to the console for analysis. we can include that in the POC scope.

[14:40] Tina Hu: earlier you mentioned encrypted logs with customer KMS - how is key rotation handled?

[14:47] Sam Patel: keys are managed by your KMS; we support key rotation and re-encryption hooks. we store envelope keys; data keys are rotated per retention window. i'll attach the KMS integration doc after the call.

[15:05] Marcus Rivera: for the POC we need to validate throughput under our traffic pattern - will the tracing slow things down under load?

[15:15] Riley Chen: tracing sampling is adaptive. for benchmarking we can run with higher sampling for a short window. the runtime is built to minimize locking - we stream traces to a worker pool. realistically you won't see significant tail latency change unless you enable token-level verbose traces for all traffic.

[15:45] Jared Lee: can we get a small runbook or playbook for debug triage?

[15:50] Alex Gomez: yes, we have a triage playbook and a pre-baked Slack/PagerDuty template. i'll include those in the follow-up.

[16:05] Riley Chen: one more tip - when investigating memory pressure or OOMs on models, the trace spans include heap and GPU memory metrics at span level if you have dedicated capacity; for hosted accounts we show aggregated host metrics.

[16:30] Priya Nair: we use OpenAI for some non-sensitive flows. curious how Redwood handles model fallbacks and routing - if a model is down do you route to a cheaper variant?

[16:42] Riley Chen: yes, routing policies can be prioritized by latency, cost, or region. automatic fallback to compatible model variants is configurable per route. we also surface the decision in the trace so you can see that a fallback happened.

[17:05] Jared Lee: any gotchas with tracing in multi-tenant setups?

[17:12] Riley Chen: isolation is enforced at the tenant level; traces are only visible to the tenant unless you share a trace id. for Dedicated/Private there's stricter network isolation.

[17:30] [Short silence while people scroll notes]

[17:45] Sam Patel: quick commercial note - POC pricing varies by traffic and whether you want dedicated capacity. i'll follow up with a POC quote after we align on the benchmark details.

[18:00] Jared Lee: sounds good. one last technical Q - can we stream traces in real time to our observability stack?

[18:08] Riley Chen: yes, we support streaming to webhooks, Kafka, or direct S3 ingestion. for Splunk/Datadog we have connectors. latency for the stream is typically sub-second to a few seconds depending on throughput.

[18:30] Priya Nair: ok let's talk POC scope - we want: 1) 2-week window, 2) 30-day retention for logs with archiving, 3) token-level traces enabled for a sample of routes, 4) canary replay tests and 5) security review.

[18:48] Sam Patel: got it. we'll propose a POC plan with timelines. next deliverables: SOC2 + network diagram, trace export examples, POC pricing, and schedule for benchmark run.

[19:05] Alex Gomez: action items captured in chat. i'll send calendar invites for a kickoff and the benchmark run once Sam shares availability.

[19:22] Jared Lee: quick note - we also want to validate SSO/JIT provisioning for RBAC. who should we loop in from your side?

[19:30] Sam Patel: i'll copy our security engineer and solutions team on the thread. Riley can lead the technical kickoff.

[19:45] [Wrap-up - summary and confirm next steps]

[20:02] Sam Patel: recap: we'll share security docs, example trace exports, and a POC plan. Riley to share the trace export and replay examples. Marcus to share redaction rules. schedule POC for week of 2026-09-22.

[20:30] Jared Lee: great, thanks everyone.

[20:35] Riley Chen: thanks - i'll follow up with the export examples in chat.

[20:40] [Call ends, people dropping off until 14:42 PDT]

Notes on transcription: auto-transcribed; occasional mis-typed product names and tech acronyms (e.g., "k v cache" for "KV cache", "rw-bison" sometimes abbreviated).
